![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14196324/assets/bd18fad0e9476915901aac297267b8d3cd652f35da0ab00325bf37ea38b17043.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$2\sqrt{2},$ as shown above. What is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =4\sqrt{2}+l+\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $4\sqrt{2},$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<4\sqrt{2}.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{32-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =32-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =32 \\ {l}^{2} & =16 \\ l & =4\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=4$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,4\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $5$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So $l=4$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =4\sqrt{2}+4+\sqrt{32-{4}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}+4+\sqrt{32-16} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}+4+\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}+4+4 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}+8 \\  & =4(2+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
